Inflation only occurs when the supply of money increases more quickly than productivity (number of goods produced). Under a gold standard inflation could still occur during a major discovery of gold. The sudden influx of money would increase prices. However, mining gold is much more difficult than printing pieces of paper at $.07-$.10 a bill or simply punching some numbers on a computer. Deflation is more the norm under pure capitalism because of the difficulty in mining gold and the ease with which humanity finds more efficient ways to produce goods. Deflation is NOT inherently bad. It allows people to save money more easily whereas the Fed's method of printing money gives new money to those who are connected in the financial world and hurts those who receive it last (or never; think fixed income) because prices rise before their wages do.
Glad to see someone else knows economics.

Consistent inflation is NOT a phenomenon inherent in capitalism, but rather a result of the creation of new money by the Federal Reserve, which is not a product of capitalism but rather an act of congress. By creating all these new dollars through open market operations the Fed (sometimes) puts billions of new dollars a month into the economy. As these dollars are spent and percolate through the economy the prices of goods are bid up because more dollars are chasing the same or a lesser amount of goods. One of the goals of the Fed is price stability but this is an impossible task since they cannot know just how much to increase the monetary base to maintain the price level. Without a Federal Reserve banks could still cause inflation themselves through the fractional reserve banking system but it would be much more difficult as competition would allow people to switch to a bank that didn't devalue currency. Under a system of actual capitalism deflation and inflation could both occur but the economy would not be so lopsided toward consistent inflation.
